news.title: Two stories, one tape: AI caution and a pipeline attack
news.summary: The day had a single dominant thread with two ends. Leaders of the biggest AI companies publicly called for slowing down frontier model development, and a Saudi oil pipeline was shut after a drone attack. The first knocked down chipmakers and the AI buildout trade; the second pushed oil sharply higher and dragged the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5% on renewed inflation worry. Both landed two days before the Fed's rate decision, which is what gave them their weight.

news.title: AI leaders call for a slower pace of development
news.summary: Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman both highlighted the safety risks of how fast AI models are advancing. There's no rule or filing behind it, just a position taken out loud, but the market read it straight through to the money that builds AI: Nvidia, Micron and the rest of the chip complex sold off, and the Nasdaq and semiconductor indexes lagged. Cybersecurity names went the other way.

news.title: Saudi Arabia shuts its East-West oil pipeline after a drone attack
news.summary: The line that lets crude bypass the Strait of Hormuz was taken offline, which removes the workaround exactly when the strait itself is the worry. Brent pushed toward $105-110 and WTI followed. Higher oil feeds directly into inflation expectations, so the bond market moved too — the 10-year yield briefly topped 5% and expectations for another Fed hike firmed.

news.title: The 10-year yield touched a multi-year high near 5%
news.summary: Bonds sold off as oil-driven inflation fears built through the session, lifting the 10-year Treasury yield to its highest in years just ahead of Wednesday's Fed decision. When yields move like this two days before a rate announcement, it's the market pre-positioning for what it thinks the Fed will say.

news.title: Indexes closed lower, but most stocks didn't
news.summary: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq both finished modestly down under the weight of AI and oil, yet the majority of individual stocks actually rose. That gap is worth noticing: the headline indexes are dominated by a handful of very large companies, so when those few are the ones being sold, the average stock can have a perfectly decent day while the number on the screen is red. Software and defensive areas did the offsetting.

news.title: Chips led the losses while cybersecurity rallied hard
news.summary: Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron and the ETFs tracking them took the brunt of the selling. CrowdStrike and its peers ran the opposite direction on the view that a world more cautious about AI spends more on protecting against it, not less — the same headline read as a cost by one group and as demand by another.

The tape read it straight through to the money that builds AI: chipmakers and datacenter suppliers sold off overnight in Asia and stayed down through the US session, while the companies that merely use AI traded green. The odd winner was cybersecurity, on the logic that an AI-risk story means more spending on protection, not less — that group roughly doubled its early gain by midday and was the strongest thing on the board.
